name: djbdns
why: Bernstein's DNS tools open a door into how DNS servers were built differently, though the package is old.

brief.what_it_is: A set of DNS programs written by D. J. Bernstein, listed on his site as 'Domain Name System tools'. The executables cover running a caching resolver (dnscache, with dnscache-conf), running authoritative servers (tinydns with tinydns-conf, tinydns-data, tinydns-edit, tinydns-get, plus axfrdns and axfr-get for zone transfer), and running walldns and rbldns servers. There are also many command-line lookup tools (dnsq, dnsip, dnsipq, dnsmx, dnsname, dnsqr, dnstxt, dnstrace, dnstracesort, dnsfilter, random-ip, pickdns). Input is DNS queries and configuration or data files; output is DNS answers and lookup results. The homepage itself is a table of contents with no one-paragraph description, so the roles above come from the page titles and the install page.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no explicit framing statement. Its contents point to a concern with DNS security and with keeping caches and servers separate, including pages titled 'The djbdns security guarantee', 'The importance of separating DNS caches from DNS servers', and 'The libresolv security disaster'.
brief.how_it_works: The install page describes building the package from source and installing it under /usr/local. It says djbdns depends on daemontools 0.70 or above and ucspi-tcp, which are what run the servers as services. The homepage's table of contents has a page on separating DNS caches from DNS servers, which suggests the design runs them as separate programs, but I did not read those pages, so I cannot describe the mechanism in detail.

brief.install_notes: Works only under UNIX. Install daemontools 0.70 or above and ucspi-tcp first. Build from the source tarball (djbdns-1.05.tar.gz), not from a package manager. Compiling on Linux may need the conf-cc workaround. The install page asks you to keep notes on what you did and what the computer did, and to include the URL of those notes in any questions sent to the dns mailing list. Local docs are optional.
brief.standout: The site is unusually long and opinionated, with how-to pages for many setups, critique pages about other DNS software and standards, and a formal 'security guarantee'. Its install steps are a plain make and make setup check, with a mail-based success report to the author instead of a package registry.
brief.status: Quiet. The install page calls djbdns-1.05 the 'latest published' package. The homepage and install page I read carry no release date or commit history, so I could not confirm a date. The scout notes also call the package old.
brief.caveats: UNIX only. The install page says SCO UnixWare is not supported. It comes with NO WARRANTY, except as stated in the security guarantee page. It needs daemontools 0.70 or above and ucspi-tcp. Linux builds may need the conf-cc workaround. The install is manual (gunzip, tar, make, make setup check) and does not use a package manager. The homepage has no one-line description, and I could not load the blurbs page (it returned 404), so my read of what each program does relies mostly on the program names and page titles.

judge.reason: A distinctive DNS suite whose separated cache and authoritative-server design offers a worthwhile way to explore how DNS infrastructure can be built differently.

entry.title: djbdns
entry.tldr: D. J. Bernstein's DNS suite: a caching resolver, authoritative servers and lookup tools, built as small separate programs with security as the stated concern.
entry.deeper_look:
djbdns is a set of DNS programs written by D. J. Bernstein. `dnscache` is a caching resolver. `tinydns` is an authoritative server, fed by `tinydns-data` and `tinydns-edit`. `axfrdns` and `axfr-get` handle zone transfers. `walldns` and `rbldns` are narrower servers. A pile of small command-line tools (`dnsq`, `dnsip`, `dnsmx`, `dnstxt`, `dnstrace`) lets you ask DNS questions and watch the answers.

The homepage is a table of contents with no summary, but the page titles show what the author cared about: 'The djbdns security guarantee', 'The importance of separating DNS caches from DNS servers', and 'The libresolv security disaster'. The suite splits the jobs of resolving and serving into different programs instead of one daemon doing everything. The brief did not cover the mechanism in detail, so read those pages for the argument.

The door here is the structure of DNS itself. Because the roles are separate, you can learn what a cache does, what an authoritative server does, and what a zone transfer is, one executable at a time. The servers run as services under `daemontools` and `ucspi-tcp`, which are the dependencies, and which are a small tour of the author's way of building Unix software.

It is old. The install page calls djbdns-1.05 the 'latest published' package, and the pages carry no release date. That does not stop it from being readable as a design.
entry.install:
brew install djbdns
# pulls in daemontools and ucspi-tcp. The upstream install is a manual source build (make, then make setup check as root) under /usr/local, and the install page says it works only under UNIX.

Shows usage for the tool that looks up IP addresses for host names.
Shows usage for the tool that traces how a name is resolved down from the root servers.

entry.whats_unique: It splits DNS into small single-purpose programs with the security argument written up on the project's own site, including pages critiquing other DNS software.
entry.caveats: Old and quiet, with no release date on the pages read, UNIX only, no warranty beyond its security guarantee, and the upstream install is manual rather than through a package manager.
